extracted.intended_audience: painters, art students, and practicing artists (particularly those studying Renaissance technique)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical guidance for achieving excellence in painting and glass-window work, drawn from Vasari's biographical and technical remarks on Raffaello and Guglielmo de Marcilla. Covers drawing, composition, anatomy, colouring, materials, and workshop practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draughtsmanship, colouring, and invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A good painter must excel in draughtsmanship, colouring, and invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari repeatedly praises combination of drawing (draughtsmanship), harmonious colouring, and inventive composition as core qualities; Raffaello is said to have improved these from his master Pietro Perugino and combined manners from several masters to form his own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of heads (male and female)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery in giving grace and movement to expressions of heads both of men and of women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leonardo is singled out as having no peer in expressions of heads; painters should study such examples to improve expression and movement in portraiture and figure heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and accurate rendering of the nude (anatomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters should study the nude thoroughly, comparing muscles of anatomical subjects and flayed bodies with the living to understand softness of flesh, muscle definition, bones, nerves, and veins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari stresses studying flayed bodies and anatomy to learn how flesh acquires softness in places and how flexures change with viewpoint; this underpins correct foreshortening and lifelike nudes. He notes Raffaello's deliberate anatomical studies to reach eminence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical invention and compositional judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to express historical inventions well and to show fine judgment in composing scenes—neither confused by too much detail nor poor from too little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition should be 'distributed with beautiful invention and order.' Raffaello focused on making scenes clear, varied, and well-ordered rather than over-imitating a single master's style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of perspectives, architecture, and landscapes
rubrics_metrics.description: Enrich scenes with a variety of perspectives, buildings, and landscapes to provide breadth to compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari lists enriching scenes with perspectives and architectural/landscape variety as essential elements that complement figure-work and narrative composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graceful treatment of drapery and clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothe figures gracefully so garments aid composition and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good painters must know how to adorn draperies, head-dresses, footwear, armour, etc., so clothes contribute to the figure's movement, dignity, and the scene's harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of light and shadow (modelling and spatial recession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use light and shadow to make figures sometimes fade into the shadows and sometimes come forward into the light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari emphasizes the painter's ability to control tonal contrasts to create depth and direct attention; Raffaello employed these to impart life and hierarchy to compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animating heads and figures (life, beauty, movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impart life and beauty to heads of women, children, young men, and old, giving them movement and boldness according to necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures should display appropriate vitality and variety; successful painters give distinctiveness and animation across age and gender in their portraits and group scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting animals, horses in motion, and martial fierceness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to depict the furious flight of horses in battles, fierceness in soldiers, and all sorts of animals convincingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari treats mastery of animals and dynamic motion (e.g., horses in flight) as technical demands every great painter should meet for historical or battle scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifelike portrait resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to give such resemblance to portraits that they seem to be alive and identifiable as the persons represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraiture requires not only likeness but liveliness; Vasari lists this among the many momentary demands of painting that distinguish the eminent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slavish imitation; pursue catholic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than blindly imitating one master (e.g., Michelangelo), cultivate a broad ('catholic') excellence across many fields of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari counsels painters who cannot match a master's strengths to seek complementary strengths elsewhere (composition, colouring, invention) and warns against over-committing to one difficult manner that lacks beauty or colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purge earlier, limiting mannerisms to learn new methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and free oneself from an early adopted manner that hampers growth, and deliberately relearn to adopt better practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raffaello had to purge Pietro Perugino's overly precise, dry draughtsmanship to learn from Michelangelo and others; Vasari presents deliberate unlearning and re-study as necessary for significant stylistic growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in use of darks (a 'middle course' in drawing and colouring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a middle course in drawing and colouring—avoid excessive use of darks which can harm beauty and relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari notes Raffaello took from Fra Bartolommeo a balanced method, combining drawing and colouring without over-darkening; excessive darkness sacrifices grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execute critical work personally rather than delegating
rubrics_metrics.description: Important works should be executed by the master with his own hand rather than entirely by assistants (especially colouring of key works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari criticizes instances where Raffaello had others colour his designs, producing work 'wanting in that grace and sweetness' characteristic of his hand; he recommends doing important execution oneself for quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'super-striving' to imitate gifts not suited to natural inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: Be satisfied with work suited to one's natural inclination; do not overreach by trying to surpass those with innate gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari warns that artists who attempt work unsuited to their nature often fail and bring shame; use judgement to choose paths where effort yields results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop conduct and collegiality as part of professional virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Courtesy, generosity, and good disposition foster unity and productive collaboration in a workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari praises Raffaello's temper, teaching, and kindness—keeping many painters employed and aiding them—arguing moral virtues contribute to artistic success and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing stained-glass windows with integrated mountings
rubrics_metrics.description: Design glass-window compositions so that lead and iron mountings fit into joinings and folds, becoming unobtrusive and giving the appearance of panel painting or relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guglielmo's windows were praised because the mountings were 'so well fitted into the joinings of the figures and the folds of the draperies, that they cannot be seen'—a technical criterion for elegant stained-glass design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour distribution for depth in stained glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the brightest colours in the foremost figures and progressively darker colours in figures as they recede to suggest depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guglielmo was noted for this practice; it achieves spatial recession in glass like in painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shading media and materials for glass painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use iron (dark) and copper (tawny) scales for shading on glass; use hematite (red) powdered and ground for burnishing gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari gives concrete materials: iron for darks (draperies, hair, buildings), copper for flesh tones, and hematite processed with gum for burnishing—practical recipe-level guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flashed-glass technique (removing layer to reveal colours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ flashing (removing a thin layer of coloured glass) and careful grinding to create layered colour effects on glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari describes flashing (e.g., placing yellow over red flashed glass) and methods of removing the top layer—either with a pointed iron (risky) or grinding with a copper wheel and emery—highlighting technique and trade-offs of safety vs skill.
